notes.meaning: God gives Moses instructions for a holy day on the first day of the seventh month. The people were to rest and hold a sacred meeting, announced by loud blasts on horns throughout the land. This blowing marked the start of the civil year and called the people to wake up, repent, and prepare for the holy days ahead.

The people were forbidden from doing their daily, ordinary jobs on this day. Instead, they had to bring special sacrifices to the Lord to be burned on the altar. Resting from regular work allowed everyone to focus on worshipping God.

God commands Israel to observe the Day of Atonement on the tenth day of the seventh month. Atonement means making things right between God and sinners by covering their guilt. The people were to gather for worship, fast, and sorrow over their sins while special offerings were presented to the Lord.

God strictly orders that no work at all be done on this sacred day. It was the special day when the high priest made atonement for the nation to cleanse them before the Lord. Because getting right with God required their full attention, all other labor had to stop.

Anyone who refused to humble themselves by fasting and repenting on this day was to be cut off from God's people. This severe punishment showed that every person was guilty before God and needed His mercy. Treating God's gift of forgiveness with careless neglect brought disastrous consequences.

The Lord Himself warns that He will personally destroy anyone who works on this solemn day. While other festivals allowed light tasks like cooking, this day required complete rest like a weekly Sabbath. God took any disregard for the day of forgiveness with the utmost seriousness.

God repeats the command that no work of any kind could be done, showing how important it was to obey. This rule was a permanent law for Israel across all their generations and in every place they lived. It reminded the people that their standing before God was not based on their own daily toil.

The Day of Atonement was to be a Sabbath of total rest and self-humbling. It began on the evening of the ninth day and lasted until the evening of the tenth day. In Israel, days were counted from sunset to sunset, so the solemn fast covered a full twenty-four hours.

God introduces the Feast of Tabernacles, which began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and lasted seven days. The word tabernacle means a temporary tent or booth. This joyful festival celebrated the end of the yearly harvest and remembered how God protected Israel during their wanderings in the desert.

The first day of the festival was set apart as a holy gathering for worship. The people were forbidden from doing any regular, heavy work. Instead, they spent the day singing praise, reading God's law, and offering sacrifices.

For seven days, fire offerings were brought daily to the Lord on the altar. Then on the eighth day, the people held another solemn holy assembly with no regular work. This closing day was a special time of thanksgiving that marked the end of the festival week and looked forward to the settled rest God gave His people.

These verses summarize the annual sacred assemblies and the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings appointed for each day. These festival sacrifices did not replace the regular weekly Sabbath worship or voluntary gifts like vow offerings and freewill offerings. Special holidays never excused God's people from their ordinary, ongoing duties to Him.

God repeats the timing of the feast, noting that it took place in autumn after the grain, grapes, and olives had all been gathered. The people were to celebrate with complete rest on both the first day and the eighth day. It was a joyful festival of thanksgiving for the abundance God provided from the land.

On the opening day, the Israelites collected branches from palm trees, leafy boughs, and willows growing by streams. They used these branches for the celebration and were commanded to rejoice before the Lord for seven full days. It was a week marked by deep joy and gratitude for God's faithful care.

The Lord commands Israel to observe this seven-day festival every year throughout all future generations. Setting aside this time each autumn ensured that the nation never forgot the Lord's goodness. It served as a lasting law to remind them that all their blessings came from God.

Every native-born Israelite was required to live in temporary booths for the seven days of the feast. This reminded later generations that God made their ancestors live in shelters after leading them out of Egypt. Living in flimsy huts prompted the people to remember their humble beginnings and thank God for His miraculous protection and guidance.

Moses faithfully delivered all of these instructions about the Lord's appointed feasts to the people of Israel. By sharing every detail, he ensured the nation understood when and how to meet with God. These festivals structured Israel's year around remembering and worshipping their Redeemer.
